old: there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Odysseus
new: there is not one of his subjects who has not forgotten Odysseus
reason: Dead 'not one … but has' syntax can read reversed. The adjudicator proposed 'every one of his subjects has forgotten Odysseus'. The lead adjusts it to mirror accepted Book 2 ¶13, where Mentor speaks the same line ('there is not one of you who has not forgotten Odysseus'). Homer repeats these lines verbatim (2.230–234 = 5.8–12), so the edition keeps them parallel. The trap word 'but' is removed either way.

old: that do their business in the waters
new: whose business is in the waters
reason: Ruling, made against Butler’s original: the modern text caused this, not Butler. Butler’s ‘occupy their business in the waters’ echoes Psalm 107:23 (‘that do business in great waters’) and renders Homer’s sea-crows ‘to whom the works of the sea are a care’ (5.66–67), birds whose work is on the water. The candidate dropped Butler’s dead verb ‘occupy’ and was left with ‘do their business’. For animals, the dominant present-day sense of that phrase is excretion, so the text now says the birds foul the water: a wrong image and an unintended joke in the Book’s set-piece description. ‘whose business is in the waters’ keeps Butler’s own noun and his ‘in the waters’ (D29). It drops only the idiom and has no scatological reading.

Butler’s hurdles are portable panels of woven withies used as fencing (Homer 5.256–257: osier wickerwork ‘to be a bulwark against the wave’). To a present-day reader, and an American one especially, ‘hurdles’ are track obstacles or difficulties, so the reader pictures the wrong object even though the sentence still seems to make sense. ‘screens’ names the same object by the function the sentence itself states (‘as a protection against the waves’). ‘wicker’ and Butler’s verb ‘fenced’ stay, so the material and the fencing survive. This replaces one word and keeps the object.

old: making them fast with braces and sheets
new: making them fast with the ropes called braces and sheets
reason: Right after Calypso's linen, 'sheets' reads as bedding and 'braces' as straps. The adjudicator's no-added-mark alternative is used: one clarifying word ('the ropes called') in narration, with Butler's two terms kept, and no em dash added (so there is no D27/D28 dividing-mark change).

old: pressing me so hard about the dead body of Achilles
new: pressing me so hard around the dead body of Achilles
reason: Butler’s ‘about’ is spatial: in Homer (5.309–310) the Trojans hurled their spears at him ‘around the dead son of Peleus’. In current English, ‘pressing someone about something’ means pressuring them on a subject. The natural reading is therefore that the Trojans were pestering him over Achilles’ body, not attacking him in the fight around it, which gets the action wrong. ‘around’ restores the spatial sense with one word. ‘so hard’ (the package’s rendering of ‘so sorely’, continuity finding 23.1) is untouched.

‘a sea’ as a countable noun for one breaking wave is sailors’ usage, and to a landsman ‘a sea broke over him’ reads oddly or as the sea in general. Homer has κῦμα, a wave (5.313). Butler also uses ‘sea’ in this paragraph for the sea itself (‘into the sea’, ‘The sea took the raft’), so the repair separates two senses that he writes with one word. It merges nothing. The two mass uses in ¶22 (‘a tremendous sea got up’, ‘what a sea the winds are raising’) mean the state of the sea, were read correctly, and are kept. The reader decoded this one, so it is optional.
verificationNote: Independent verification R1: unnecessary. The BEFORE 'a sea broke over him' was clear, the reader understood it, and 'a sea' is Butler's own word, still current nautical English for a heavy wave. Reverted.

old: both sail and yard went over
new: both sail and yardarm went over
reason: On its own, ‘yard’ reads as a garden or as three feet, and then ‘sail and yard went over into the sea’ describes nothing. It is the spar Butler calls ‘yard arm’ when Odysseus makes it in ¶19 (candidate ‘yardarm’, which the reader decoded), and Homer uses one word for it in both places (ἐπίκριον, 5.254 and 5.318). Reusing the ¶19 word restores the link and the picture (the mast snapped, the sail and its spar gone) with one word.

‘stay’ in the sense ‘stop’ is dead (it is on the brief’s sweep list). In current English, ‘the god stayed his stream’ either fails to parse or means ‘remained’. Homer: ‘he stopped his current and held back the wave’ (5.451). The edition already renders Butler’s ‘stay’ (= stop) as ‘stop’ elsewhere: 3 ¶26 ‘stopped them’, 4 ¶2 ‘stopped their horses’, 24 ¶42 ‘did not stop it’. This instance survived only because the package treated ‘staid’ → ‘stayed’ as a spelling change (continuity §5). ‘stopped his stream and stilled the waves’ also keeps Butler’s st-/st- pairing. The reader decoded it, so it is optional, but it brings the edition into line with itself.

new: hides a burning brand as fire-seed
reason: The Book’s last simile turns on this object. A man buries a smoldering piece of firewood in the ashes to keep his fire alive, as Odysseus buries himself in leaves (Homer 5.488–490, δαλός). The dominant present-day sense of ‘brand’ is a trademark, so the simile’s key noun means nothing until the reader works back from ‘ashes’. One adjective, folded into the narration, makes the sense unmistakable and keeps Butler’s noun, ‘fire-seed’ and the whole image.
